title: Philosophy
blurb: Big questions, ethics, the mind, ways to live and good arguments.

cards.title: What philosophy is
cards.text: Philosophy means "love of wisdom". It asks questions science can't settle by experiment alone: what is real, what can we know, how should we live?

cards.title: Before Socrates
cards.text: The first Greek philosophers looked for natural explanations instead of myths. Thales said everything was water; Heraclitus said everything flows; Democritus imagined atoms.

cards.title: Socrates
cards.text: Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) wrote nothing. He questioned people in the streets of Athens until they saw the gaps in what they thought they knew. Athens sentenced him to death.

cards.title: "I know that I know nothing"
cards.text: Socrates' wisdom was knowing the limits of his knowledge. "The unexamined life is not worth living" is his best-known line, from Plato's *Apology*.

cards.title: Plato's cave
cards.text: Plato imagined prisoners chained in a cave who see only shadows on the wall and take them for reality. Philosophy is the painful climb out into the sunlight.

cards.title: Plato's Forms
cards.text: Plato believed that behind changing things are perfect, eternal Forms: many circles exist, but each is an imperfect copy of the perfect Circle we understand with reason.

cards.title: Aristotle
cards.text: Plato's student Aristotle (384–322 BCE) studied almost everything: logic, biology, physics, politics, poetry. He tutored Alexander the Great and founded the Lyceum.

cards.title: The golden mean
cards.text: For Aristotle, virtue sits between two extremes. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between stinginess and wastefulness.

cards.title: Eudaimonia
cards.text: Aristotle's aim of life was eudaimonia, often translated as flourishing: living well by using reason and practising virtue, not just feeling good.

cards.title: The Socratic method today

items: What do you mean by that?

cards.text: Teachers, lawyers and coaches still use Socratic questioning: instead of giving answers, they ask questions that help you examine your own reasoning.

quiz.q: What did Socrates claim to know?
quiz.explain: Knowing your limits is the start of wisdom.

quiz.q: In Plato's cave, what do the prisoners see?
For Aristotle, courage lies between…

lessons.title: Ethics
lessons.summary: How should we decide what's right?

cards.title: Three big theories
cards.text: Most ethical theories focus on one of three things: the consequences of an action, the duties or rules involved, or the character of the person acting.

cards.title: Utilitarianism
cards.text: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the right action produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.

cards.title: Kant's duty

items.r: "Could everyone lie whenever it helps? Then trust collapses"

cards.text: Immanuel Kant argued some things are wrong whatever the consequences. His test: act only on a rule you could want everyone to follow.

cards.title: People as ends
cards.text: Kant also said: never treat people merely as a means to your goals, but always also as ends in themselves, with their own dignity.

cards.title: Virtue ethics
cards.text: Rather than asking "what rule applies?", virtue ethics asks "what would a good person do?" and focuses on building traits like honesty, courage and kindness.

cards.title: The trolley problem
cards.text: A runaway trolley will kill five people. You can pull a lever to divert it, killing one instead. Most people would pull. But would you push someone off a bridge to stop it? Most say no.

cards.title: Moral luck
cards.text: Two drivers text at the wheel; one hits a child, the other gets home safely. Their choices were equally bad, but we judge them very differently.

cards.title: The veil of ignorance
cards.text: John Rawls asked: what society would you design if you didn't know who you'd be in it, rich or poor, healthy or ill? He thought you'd protect the worst off.

cards.title: Is and ought
cards.text: David Hume noticed that you can't get an "ought" from an "is" alone. "Smoking harms health" doesn't by itself mean "you shouldn't smoke"; you need a value too.

cards.title: A hard choice
cards.text: A doctor has five patients needing organs and one healthy visitor. A utilitarian sum seems to say sacrifice one; nearly everyone says no. Testing theories against cases is how ethics progresses.

quiz.q: Which theory judges actions by their consequences?
quiz.explain: The greatest happiness for the greatest number.

quiz.q: What is Rawls' "veil of ignorance"?
options: Designing society without knowing your place in it

lessons.title: Mind and knowledge
lessons.summary: What can we know? What is a mind?

cards.title: Descartes' doubt
cards.text: René Descartes tried to doubt everything: senses can deceive, dreams feel real. The one thing he couldn't doubt was that he was doubting: "I think, therefore I am."

cards.title: Rationalists vs empiricists
cards.text: Rationalists like Descartes said knowledge comes mainly from reason. Empiricists like Locke and Hume said it comes from experience; the mind starts as a blank slate.

cards.title: The problem of induction
cards.text: The Sun has risen every day, so we expect it tomorrow. Hume pointed out we can't prove that the future will be like the past; we just assume it.

cards.title: Falsifiability
cards.text: Karl Popper argued a scientific theory must be testable in a way that could prove it wrong. "All swans are white" is scientific: one black swan refutes it.

cards.title: The mind–body problem
cards.text: How does the physical brain produce thoughts and feelings? Dualists say mind and body are different things; physicalists say the mind is what the brain does.

cards.title: The hard problem
cards.text: Philosopher David Chalmers asked why brain activity feels like anything at all. Explaining what the brain does is "easy"; explaining why there's an inner experience is "hard".

cards.title: What is it like to be a bat?

steps: Know every fact about bat brains

cards.text: Thomas Nagel argued that even knowing everything about a bat's echolocation wouldn't tell us what it's like to experience it from the inside.

cards.title: The Chinese room
cards.text: John Searle imagined a person following a rulebook to answer Chinese questions perfectly without understanding Chinese. Does a computer understand, or just manipulate symbols?

cards.title: Personal identity
cards.text: If every plank of a ship is replaced over time, is it the same ship? Your cells renew too. What makes you the same person over your life: memory, body, or something else?

cards.title: Thinking about AI
cards.text: These old puzzles are now practical: can a language model understand, or have experiences? Philosophers disagree, and the Chinese room is quoted in AI debates every week.

quiz.q: What couldn't Descartes doubt?
According to Popper, a scientific theory must be…

cards.title: Stoicism
cards.text: Stoics like Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus Aurelius taught that we can't control events, only our judgements and actions. Peace comes from focusing on what's up to us.

cards.title: The dichotomy of control
cards.text: Before worrying, sort the problem: can I control it, influence it or neither? Spend energy only on the first two.

cards.title: Negative visualisation
cards.text: Stoics imagined losing what they had, not to be gloomy, but to appreciate it more and be ready for setbacks.

cards.title: Epicureanism
cards.text: Epicurus taught that a good life is a pleasant one, but meant simple pleasures: friends, conversation, bread and water, and freedom from fear and pain, not luxury.

cards.title: Buddhist philosophy
cards.text: The Buddha taught that suffering comes from craving and attachment, and that a path of ethical living, mindfulness and wisdom can lead beyond it.

cards.title: Confucius
cards.text: Confucius (551–479 BCE) emphasised good relationships, respect, education and self-cultivation. His golden rule: "Do not do to others what you would not want done to you."

cards.title: Existentialism
cards.text: Jean-Paul Sartre said "existence precedes essence": we aren't born with a fixed purpose; we create ourselves through our choices and are responsible for them.

cards.title: The absurd

steps: Push again, and find joy in it

cards.text: Albert Camus described the absurd: our search for meaning in a universe that offers none. His answer, from *The Myth of Sisyphus*: keep living fully anyway.

cards.title: Pessoa's many selves
cards.text: Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa wrote as dozens of "heteronyms", such as Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Álvaro de Campos, each with its own life and philosophy.

cards.title: A Stoic morning

items: How do I want to respond?

cards.text: Marcus Aurelius reminded himself each morning that he'd meet difficult people today, and that he could still choose to act well. A one-minute plan for the day ahead.

quiz.q: What did the Stoics say we can control?
quiz.explain: Focus on what's up to you.

quiz.q: What did Epicurus mean by pleasure?
options: Simple pleasures and freedom from fear

lessons.title: Arguments and fallacies
lessons.summary: How to reason well and spot bad arguments.

cards.title: What an argument is
cards.text: An argument gives reasons (premises) for a conclusion. It's good if the premises are true and actually support the conclusion.

cards.title: Valid vs sound
cards.text: An argument is valid if the conclusion must follow from the premises; sound if it's valid and the premises are true. "All cats fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom flies" is valid but not sound.

cards.title: Deduction vs induction
cards.text: Deduction moves from general rules to certain conclusions. Induction moves from observations to probable generalisations.

cards.title: Ad hominem
cards.text: Attacking the person instead of the argument. "You can't trust his climate data; he drives a big car" doesn't touch the data.

cards.title: Straw man
cards.text: Misrepresenting someone's view to make it easier to attack. "You want speed limits? So you want everyone to walk?"

cards.title: False dilemma
cards.text: Presenting only two options when more exist. "Either you're with us or against us" ignores the many positions in between.

cards.title: Slippery slope

steps: Disaster, with no evidence for each link

cards.text: Claiming one small step will inevitably lead to a disaster, without showing why. Sometimes slopes are real; the fallacy is assuming them.

cards.title: Appeal to popularity
cards.text: "Millions of people believe it, so it must be true." Popularity isn't evidence; many popular beliefs have turned out false.

cards.title: Correlation vs causation
cards.text: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, but ice cream doesn't cause drowning: hot weather drives both. A link doesn't prove one causes the other.

cards.title: Steelmanning
cards.text: The opposite of a straw man: state your opponent's view in its strongest form before replying. If they'd say "yes, that's exactly my view", you're ready to disagree.

quiz.q: "You can't trust her argument, she's not an expert." What fallacy?
quiz.explain: Attacks the person, not the argument.

quiz.q: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. This shows…

cards.title: The state of nature
cards.text: Philosophers imagined life without any government to ask why we accept rulers. Their answers shaped modern democracies.

cards.title: Hobbes' Leviathan
cards.text: Thomas Hobbes (1651) argued that without a powerful sovereign, people would live in a war of all against all. We trade freedom for security.

cards.title: Locke and rights
cards.text: John Locke argued people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government that violates them can be replaced. He influenced the American founders.

cards.title: Rousseau's general will
cards.text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau began *The Social Contract* (1762) with "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains". He sought a society governed by the common good.

cards.title: Separation of powers
cards.text: Montesquieu argued liberty requires dividing power between legislative, executive and judicial branches, each checking the others. Portugal's constitution follows this idea.

cards.title: Mill's harm principle
cards.text: John Stuart Mill argued the only reason to restrict someone's freedom is to prevent harm to others, not to protect them from themselves.

cards.title: Liberalism and socialism
cards.text: Broadly, liberal traditions emphasise individual rights and markets; socialist traditions emphasise equality and collective ownership. Most modern democracies mix both.

cards.title: Conservatism
cards.text: Edmund Burke valued tradition and gradual change, warning that institutions hold wisdom built over generations that radical reforms can destroy.

cards.title: Democracy's critics
cards.text: Plato worried that democracy lets persuasion beat wisdom. Churchill later quipped that democracy is the worst form of government, except for all the others.

cards.title: Portugal's democracy
cards.text: After nearly 50 years of dictatorship, the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 restored freedom, with a new constitution in 1976.

quiz.q: Who described life without government as "nasty, brutish and short"?
What is Mill's harm principle?
options: Freedom can only be restricted to prevent harm to others

quiz.q: Who proposed separating legislative, executive and judicial powers?

cards.title: The question
cards.text: If every event has a cause, including the firing of your neurons, are your choices truly free? Or is free will an illusion?

cards.title: Determinism
cards.text: Determinism says everything that happens is fixed by prior causes and the laws of nature. Given the past, only one future is possible.

cards.title: Libertarian free will
cards.text: Some philosophers argue we have genuine freedom that isn't fully determined by prior causes. Critics ask how a choice can be both uncaused and controlled.

cards.title: Compatibilism
cards.text: Most philosophers are compatibilists: free will means acting on your own reasons without coercion, even if those reasons have causes.

cards.title: Libet's experiment
cards.text: In the 1980s, Benjamin Libet found brain activity began before people reported deciding to move. Its meaning is fiercely debated; later work questions the interpretation.

cards.title: Quantum randomness?
cards.text: Quantum physics suggests some events are truly random. But randomness doesn't seem to give us control either.

cards.title: Moral responsibility
cards.text: If free will is an illusion, can we blame or praise people? Many think responsibility still makes sense for guiding behaviour and protecting others.

cards.title: Frankfurt's cases
cards.text: Harry Frankfurt imagined someone who would have been forced to choose X anyway, but chose X freely on their own. Are they responsible? Most say yes.

cards.title: Feeling free
cards.text: Whatever the metaphysics, we experience deliberating and choosing. Some argue that experience is part of what freedom means for creatures like us.

cards.title: Practical freedom
cards.text: Even if causes shape us, we can shape future causes: choosing environments, habits and friends that make better choices easier.

quiz.q: What do compatibilists believe?
quiz.explain: Acting on your own reasons without coercion.

quiz.q: What did Libet's experiment seem to show?
options: Brain activity before the felt decision

cards.title: Meaning given or made?
cards.text: Some traditions hold that meaning is given by God or nature; others, like existentialism, that we create our own meaning.

cards.title: Religious answers
cards.text: Many religions locate life's meaning in a relationship with God, following a path or escaping a cycle of rebirth.

cards.title: Aristotle again
cards.text: For Aristotle, a meaningful life is one of flourishing: using our capacities well, in a community, guided by virtue.

cards.title: Nihilism
cards.text: Nihilism holds that life has no inherent meaning. Nietzsche warned of it and urged people to create new values rather than despair.

cards.title: Camus' answer
cards.text: Camus said the honest response to a meaningless universe is revolt: to live fully, passionately and freely anyway. "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."

cards.title: Frankl's search
cards.text: Psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who survived Nazi concentration camps, argued meaning comes from work, love and the attitude we take to unavoidable suffering.

cards.title: Ikigai

items: What you can be paid for

cards.text: The Japanese idea of ikigai is often described as a reason for being. Western diagrams combining love, skill, need and pay are a modern addition.

cards.title: Meaning vs happiness
cards.text: Studies suggest meaning and happiness overlap but differ: happiness is about the present and getting; meaning links past, present and future, and giving.

cards.title: Small meanings
cards.text: Many people find meaning not in one grand answer but in everyday things: family, friends, work done well, beauty and helping others.

cards.title: A reflective exercise
cards.text: Imagine your 80th birthday. What would you want the people closest to you to say about how you lived? That points to what matters to you.

quiz.q: Who wrote "one must imagine Sisyphus happy"?
According to Viktor Frankl, where can meaning come from?
options: Work, love and our attitude to suffering

cards.title: The scientific method
cards.text: Science proceeds by observation, hypothesis, prediction and testing. Results that contradict predictions force revision.

cards.title: Bacon's induction
cards.text: Francis Bacon (1620) urged gathering careful observations and building general laws from them, rather than reasoning from authority.

cards.title: Popper's falsification
cards.text: Karl Popper argued science advances by trying to refute theories. A theory that survives many attempts is corroborated, not proven.

cards.title: Kuhn's revolutions
cards.text: Thomas Kuhn (1962) argued science works within paradigms. Anomalies pile up until a revolution replaces the old framework, like Copernicus over Ptolemy.

cards.title: Occam's razor
cards.text: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits the evidence. Extra assumptions need extra justification.

cards.title: Correlation and causation
cards.text: Science uses controlled experiments to separate cause from coincidence: change one thing, keep everything else equal, and see what happens.

cards.title: Peer review
cards.text: Before publication, other experts check a study's methods and conclusions. It catches many errors, though not all.

cards.title: Pseudoscience
cards.text: Astrology and homeopathy make claims that can't be tested or keep failing tests. Hallmarks include vague predictions and ignoring contrary evidence.

cards.title: Models are maps
cards.text: Scientific models simplify reality to make predictions. Statistician George Box said "all models are wrong, but some are useful".

cards.title: Science corrects itself
cards.text: Science's strength isn't certainty but self-correction. Theories are revised when better evidence arrives, as when continental drift was accepted in the 1960s.

quiz.q: What is Occam's razor?
options: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits

quiz.q: According to Kuhn, what triggers a scientific revolution?
quiz.explain: The old paradigm can't explain them.

lessons.title: Eastern philosophy
lessons.summary: Wisdom from India, China and Japan.

cards.title: Laozi and the Tao
cards.text: The *Tao Te Ching*, attributed to Laozi, teaches living in harmony with the Tao, the natural way, through simplicity, humility and effortless action (wu wei).

cards.title: Yin and yang
cards.text: Yin and yang describe complementary opposites that depend on each other: dark and light, rest and activity. Balance between them matters.

cards.title: Confucian relationships
cards.text: Confucius stressed five key relationships, each with mutual duties, as the basis of a harmonious society.

cards.title: Hindu philosophy
cards.text: Hindu traditions explore dharma (duty), karma (action and consequence), samsara (rebirth) and moksha (liberation).

cards.title: The Bhagavad Gita
cards.text: In the Gita, the warrior Arjuna hesitates before battle. Krishna teaches him to act according to duty without attachment to results.

cards.title: Four Noble Truths
cards.text: The Buddha taught that life involves suffering; suffering arises from craving; it can end; and the Eightfold Path leads there.

cards.title: Impermanence
cards.text: Buddhism stresses that everything changes, including the self. Clinging to what can't last causes suffering.

cards.title: Zen
cards.text: Zen Buddhism, from China to Japan, emphasises meditation and direct experience over study. Koans like "what is the sound of one hand clapping?" jolt the mind.

cards.title: Mindfulness today
cards.text: Modern mindfulness practices adapt Buddhist meditation for stress reduction. Studies show modest benefits for anxiety, stress and focus.

cards.title: East meets West
cards.text: Schopenhauer drew on Indian thought; Stoicism resembles Buddhism in places. Many questions about suffering, self and virtue are shared across cultures.

quiz.q: What is "wu wei" in Taoism?
options: Effortless action in harmony with nature

quiz.q: According to the Buddha, what causes suffering?

lessons.title: Medieval philosophy
lessons.summary: Faith and reason in the Middle Ages.

cards.title: Augustine
cards.text: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) blended Christian faith with Plato's ideas. His *Confessions* is one of the first great autobiographies, exploring memory, time and the self.

cards.title: The problem of evil
cards.text: If God is all-powerful and all-good, why does evil exist? Augustine answered that evil is an absence of good, partly caused by human free will.

cards.title: Boethius
cards.text: Writing in prison awaiting execution in 524, Boethius wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy*: Lady Philosophy teaches that true happiness can't be taken away by fortune.

cards.title: Islamic golden age
cards.text: Scholars like Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes (Ibn Rushd) preserved and developed Greek philosophy. Their commentaries on Aristotle shaped European thought.

cards.title: Avicenna's floating man

steps: The self is not the body?

cards.text: Avicenna imagined a man created floating in the air, blindfolded, touching nothing. He would still know he exists: self-awareness without the senses.

cards.title: Maimonides
cards.text: Moses Maimonides, a Jewish philosopher born in Córdoba, sought to reconcile faith with Aristotle's reason in his *Guide for the Perplexed*.

cards.title: Thomas Aquinas
cards.text: Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) combined Aristotle with Christian theology, arguing faith and reason can't truly conflict because both come from God.

cards.title: Five ways
cards.text: Aquinas offered five arguments for God's existence, including the "first mover": everything that moves is moved by something, so there must be a first, unmoved mover.

cards.title: Ockham's razor
cards.text: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) argued we shouldn't multiply entities beyond necessity. His principle became the famous "razor".

cards.title: Universities
cards.text: Medieval Europe founded universities, including Coimbra in 1290, one of the oldest in continuous operation in the world. Philosophy and theology were at their core.

quiz.q: Who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison?
What did Aquinas believe about faith and reason?
When was Portugal's first university founded?
quiz.explain: In Lisbon, later moved to Coimbra.

cards.title: Dare to know
cards.text: Kant defined the Enlightenment in 1784 as humanity's emergence from self-imposed immaturity. His motto: *Sapere aude*, dare to think for yourself.

cards.title: Spinoza
cards.text: Baruch Spinoza, of Portuguese-Jewish descent, identified God with Nature itself, and argued for freedom of thought. He was expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656.

cards.title: Voltaire
cards.text: Voltaire attacked intolerance and religious persecution with wit. The 1755 Lisbon earthquake inspired his *Candide*, mocking the idea that this is the "best of all possible worlds".

cards.title: Hume's scepticism

items: The self is a bundle of perceptions

cards.text: David Hume doubted that we can know causes, the self or miracles with certainty. Kant said Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber".

cards.title: Kant's synthesis
cards.text: Kant argued the mind actively structures experience with space, time and causality. We know things as they appear to us, not as they are in themselves.

cards.title: The Encyclopédie
cards.text: Diderot and d'Alembert's *Encyclopédie* (1751–1772) gathered human knowledge, including crafts and sciences, to spread reason widely.

cards.title: Wollstonecraft
cards.text: Mary Wollstonecraft's *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* (1792) argued women appear inferior only because they're denied education.

cards.title: Adam Smith
cards.text: Adam Smith, a moral philosopher, argued in 1776 that self-interest in free markets can benefit society, like an "invisible hand". He also wrote about sympathy and ethics.

cards.title: Revolutions
cards.text: Enlightenment ideas about rights and consent of the governed fed the American Revolution (1776) and the French Revolution (1789).

cards.title: Pombal's reforms
cards.text: In Portugal, the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt Lisbon and pushed Enlightenment-style reforms: modernising Coimbra University, secular schooling and science, though he ruled with an iron hand.

quiz.q: Which disaster inspired Voltaire's Candide?
What was Kant's Enlightenment motto?

cards.title: Hegel's dialectic
cards.text: Hegel saw history as ideas developing through conflict: a position meets its opposite, and a higher synthesis emerges.

cards.title: Marx
cards.text: Karl Marx argued history is driven by economic conflict between classes, and that capitalism exploits workers. His ideas inspired movements and regimes with very different outcomes.

cards.title: Mill's utilitarianism
cards.text: John Stuart Mill refined utilitarianism, arguing some pleasures are higher than others: "better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied".

cards.title: Kierkegaard
cards.text: Søren Kierkegaard, the "father of existentialism", stressed individual choice, commitment and the anxiety of freedom. Truth, he said, must be lived.

cards.title: Schopenhauer
cards.text: Arthur Schopenhauer saw life driven by a blind, restless "will" that causes endless desire and suffering. Art, compassion and asceticism offer relief.

cards.title: Nietzsche's "God is dead"
cards.text: Friedrich Nietzsche's famous line meant that belief in God no longer anchored Western values, and people must face creating new values.

cards.title: The Übermensch
cards.text: Nietzsche's ideal is a person who creates their own values and affirms life fully. Later misuse of his ideas by the Nazis distorted them.

cards.title: Eternal recurrence
cards.text: Nietzsche's thought experiment: if you had to live your life again exactly, infinitely, would you rejoice or despair? Live so you'd say yes.

cards.title: Pragmatism
cards.text: American pragmatists like William James argued an idea's truth lies in its practical consequences: what difference does it make in practice?

cards.title: Darwin's impact
cards.text: Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) challenged ideas of human uniqueness and purpose in nature, reshaping philosophy, religion and ethics.

quiz.q: What did Nietzsche mean by "God is dead"?
options: Belief no longer anchors Western values

quiz.q: Who said it's better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied?

cards.title: What they're for
cards.text: Thought experiments test ideas by imagining scenarios we can't (or shouldn't) run for real. They reveal hidden assumptions.

cards.title: The ship of Theseus
cards.text: If every plank of a ship is replaced, is it the same ship? And if you rebuild the old planks into a ship, which is the original?

cards.title: Brain in a vat
cards.text: How do you know you're not a brain in a vat, fed experiences by a computer? It updates Descartes' doubt for the age of simulation.

cards.title: Experience machine
cards.text: Robert Nozick asked: would you plug into a machine giving you any pleasurable experience you want, for life? Most say no, suggesting we value more than pleasure.

cards.title: Mary's room

steps: Sees red for the first time

cards.text: Mary knows every physical fact about colour but has lived in a black-and-white room. When she first sees red, does she learn something new?

cards.title: The teleporter
cards.text: A teleporter scans you, destroys you and builds an exact copy on Mars. Is the copy you? What if the original isn't destroyed?

cards.title: Newcomb's problem
cards.text: A predictor who is almost always right offers two boxes: one with €1,000, one with €1 million or nothing. Take both, or just the second? Philosophers split.

cards.title: The original position
cards.text: Rawls asked what principles you'd choose for society from behind a veil of ignorance. It's a thought experiment about fairness.

cards.title: Galileo's falling bodies

steps: Should be both faster and slower

cards.text: Galileo imagined tying a heavy and light stone together: would they fall faster or slower? The contradiction showed all objects fall at the same rate.

cards.title: Einstein's light beam
cards.text: Aged 16, Einstein imagined chasing a light beam. What would he see? The puzzle led him to special relativity.

quiz.q: What does Nozick's experience machine suggest?
options: We value more than pleasant experiences

quiz.q: What did Galileo's thought experiment show?
options: All objects fall at the same rate

cards.title: Technology isn't neutral
cards.text: Tools shape behaviour: cars shaped cities, phones shaped attention. Designers make value choices, whether they realise it or not.

cards.title: Privacy
cards.text: Who owns your data? Philosophers argue privacy protects freedom, dignity and the ability to think without being watched. The EU's GDPR gave people rights over their data.

cards.title: Algorithmic bias
cards.text: AI trained on biased historical data can repeat the bias: hiring tools that favoured men because past hires were mostly men.

cards.title: Who's responsible?
cards.text: If a self-driving car crashes, who's to blame: the owner, the manufacturer, the programmer or the AI? Responsibility gets spread thin.

cards.title: The trolley problem, automated
cards.text: Self-driving cars make the trolley problem real. MIT's Moral Machine survey collected millions of answers and found preferences differed across cultures.

cards.title: Automation and work
cards.text: If machines do most jobs, how do we share the wealth, and where will people find meaning? Proposals include retraining, shorter weeks and universal basic income.

cards.title: AI alignment
cards.text: How do we make sure powerful AI systems pursue goals humans actually want? Even well-meant instructions can be misread, like King Midas' golden touch.

cards.title: Can AI be conscious?
cards.text: Philosophers disagree whether AI could have experiences. If it could, would it have moral status? The question shapes how we should treat future systems.

cards.title: Deepfakes and truth
cards.text: Realistic fake images, voices and videos make it harder to trust what we see. Verification, provenance labels and media literacy become vital.

cards.title: Questions to ask of any tech
cards.text: Who benefits? Who might be harmed? What happens if everyone uses it? Can it be undone? These simple questions guide responsible use.

quiz.q: Why can AI systems be biased?
options: They learn from biased historical data
quiz.explain: Biased data in, biased decisions out.

quiz.q: What is AI alignment about?
options: Making AI pursue goals humans actually want

lessons.title: Language and meaning
lessons.summary: How words connect to the world.

cards.title: Words and things
cards.text: How does the word "cat" come to mean cats? Philosophers of language ask how symbols get meaning, and how we understand each other at all.

cards.title: Sense and reference
cards.text: Gottlob Frege noted that "the morning star" and "the evening star" refer to the same thing, Venus, but have different senses, ways of presenting it.

cards.title: Wittgenstein's early view
cards.text: In the *Tractatus* (1921), Wittgenstein argued language pictures facts, and "whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent".

cards.title: Meaning is use
cards.text: Later, Wittgenstein changed his mind: the meaning of a word is its use in a "language game". "Water!" means different things to a thirsty person and a firefighter.

cards.title: Family resemblance
cards.text: What do all games have in common? Nothing single, Wittgenstein said; they share overlapping similarities, like family members' faces.

cards.title: Speech acts
cards.text: J.L. Austin noticed some sentences do things: "I promise", "I resign", "I now pronounce you married" perform an action by being said.

cards.title: Implicature
cards.text: Paul Grice noticed we mean more than we say. A reference letter saying only "he has neat handwriting" says a lot by what it leaves out.

cards.title: Language shapes thought?
cards.text: The Sapir–Whorf idea suggests language influences how we think. Strong versions are rejected, but language can nudge attention, like Russian speakers distinguishing light and dark blue faster.

cards.title: Saudade
cards.text: Some words seem untranslatable. Portuguese *saudade*, a longing for something absent that may never return, is often cited, though the feeling itself is universal.

cards.title: Machines and meaning

items: words need contact with the world

cards.text: Large language models produce fluent text by learning patterns in huge amounts of language. Whether they understand meaning, or just use, revives old debates.

quiz.q: What did the later Wittgenstein say about meaning?
"I promise" is an example of…
What is Grice's implicature?
options: Meaning more than you literally say

cards.title: What is beauty?
cards.text: Is beauty in the object or in the eye of the beholder? Philosophers have argued both ways for 2,500 years.

cards.title: Plato on art

steps: Painting of a bed: copy of a copy

cards.text: Plato distrusted art as a copy of a copy: a painting imitates a bed, which itself imitates the Form of Bed. He would have censored poets in his ideal city.

cards.title: Aristotle's catharsis
cards.text: Aristotle defended tragedy: watching suffering on stage arouses pity and fear and purges them, a cleansing he called catharsis.

cards.title: Hume's standard of taste
cards.text: Hume argued taste varies, but some judges are better: those with practice, delicacy, comparison and freedom from prejudice. Their agreement forms a standard.

cards.title: Kant on beauty
cards.text: Kant said a judgement of beauty is disinterested, not about wanting the thing, yet claims everyone should agree, unlike "I like sugar".

cards.title: The sublime
cards.text: The sublime is the awe mixed with fear we feel before vast or powerful things: storms, mountains, the night sky. Burke and Kant both explored it.

cards.title: What is art?
cards.text: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp exhibited a urinal signed "R. Mutt" as art. Is art defined by beauty, skill, intention or by the art world accepting it?

cards.title: Expression
cards.text: Tolstoy argued art is the transmission of feelings: the artist feels something and expresses it so others feel it too.

cards.title: Ugly art
cards.text: Art doesn't have to be beautiful. Goya's *Black Paintings* and war photography disturb us, yet they can be powerful and important.

cards.title: Looking slowly
cards.text: Spend ten minutes with one painting: what do you notice first? After five minutes? Slow looking reveals far more than the average museum glance of under 30 seconds.

quiz.q: What was Aristotle's view of tragedy?
What did Duchamp exhibit as art in 1917?

cards.title: The big questions
cards.text: Does God exist? Can faith be rational? Why is there something rather than nothing? These questions are explored with argument, not just belief.

cards.title: Cosmological argument

steps: Everything that begins has a cause

cards.text: Everything that begins has a cause; the universe began; so it has a cause. Critics ask why the cause must be God, and what caused God.

cards.title: Design argument
cards.text: William Paley (1802): if you found a watch on a heath, you'd infer a designer; nature is far more complex, so it needs one too. Darwin offered another explanation.

cards.title: Ontological argument
cards.text: Anselm (1078) argued God is "that than which nothing greater can be conceived", and something that exists is greater than something only imagined. Kant replied that existence isn't a property.

cards.title: Pascal's wager
cards.text: Blaise Pascal argued it's rational to believe: if God exists you gain everything; if not, you lose little. Critics ask which god, and whether belief can be chosen.

cards.title: The problem of evil again
cards.text: The existence of suffering is the strongest argument against an all-good, all-powerful God. Responses appeal to free will, growth or mystery.

cards.title: Faith and reason
cards.text: Some say faith goes beyond reason; others that it must be reasonable; others that it's a matter of trust, like trusting a friend.

cards.title: Atheism and agnosticism
cards.text: Atheists believe there's no God; agnostics hold we can't know. Bertrand Russell compared the burden of proof to an invisible teapot orbiting the Sun.

cards.title: Religious experience
cards.text: Many people report direct experiences of the divine. William James studied them in 1902. Are they evidence of God, or of the human brain?

cards.title: Why something?
cards.text: Leibniz asked: why is there something rather than nothing? Physics, theology and philosophy offer answers, but none is universally accepted.

quiz.q: What is Pascal's wager?
options: Belief is rational given the stakes

quiz.q: How did Darwin challenge Paley's design argument?

lessons.title: Justice and rights
lessons.summary: What do we owe each other?

cards.title: What is justice?

items: justice is harmony and good for the soul

cards.text: In Plato's *Republic*, Thrasymachus claims justice is just the interest of the stronger. Socrates spends the whole book trying to prove him wrong.

cards.title: Distributive justice
cards.text: How should wealth and opportunities be shared? Philosophers propose equality, need, merit, free exchange or helping the worst off.

cards.title: Rawls' difference principle

steps: Does it help the worst off?

cards.text: Rawls argued inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the least advantaged, such as higher pay for doctors that results in better healthcare for all.

cards.title: Nozick's entitlement
cards.text: Robert Nozick replied that if holdings were acquired fairly and transferred freely, the result is just, even if unequal. Taxation for redistribution, he argued, is like forced labour.

cards.title: Human rights
cards.text: After the Second World War, the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), setting rights for all people regardless of nation.

cards.title: Rights and duties
cards.text: Every right implies duties: your right to free speech implies others' duty not to silence you. Some rights demand action, like education.

cards.title: Punishment
cards.text: Why punish? To give people what they deserve (retribution), to prevent future crimes (deterrence), to protect society, or to reform the offender.

cards.title: Restorative justice
cards.text: Restorative justice brings offenders and victims together to repair harm, rather than just punishing. Studies show it often satisfies victims more.

cards.title: Global justice
cards.text: Peter Singer argued that if you'd ruin your shoes to save a child drowning in a pond, you should give to save distant children too. Distance shouldn't matter morally.

cards.title: Fair sharing
cards.text: Two children share a cake: one cuts, the other chooses. Both get a fair deal without trusting each other: a simple mechanism for justice.

quiz.q: What did Rawls' difference principle say?
options: Inequality only if it helps the worst off

quiz.q: What's the fair way for two children to share a cake?
quiz.explain: It makes the cutter cut evenly.

lessons.title: Time and existence
lessons.summary: What is real, what is now?

cards.title: What is time?
cards.text: Augustine wrote: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I know not." It's still puzzling.

cards.title: Presentism vs eternalism
cards.text: Presentists say only the present exists. Eternalists say past, present and future are equally real, like places on a map; relativity seems to support them.

cards.title: The arrow of time
cards.text: Physics laws mostly work the same backwards, yet we remember the past, not the future, and eggs break but don't unbreak. Entropy gives time its direction.

cards.title: Zeno's arrow
cards.text: Zeno argued a flying arrow is motionless at every instant, so motion is impossible. Calculus later explained how motion emerges from instants.

cards.title: Heraclitus' river
cards.text: "You can't step in the same river twice," said Heraclitus: the water has flowed on, and you've changed too. Reality is change.

cards.title: Parmenides' stillness
cards.text: Parmenides argued the opposite: change is an illusion, and true reality is one, unchanging and eternal.

cards.title: Why is there now?
cards.text: Physics has no special "now", yet we experience one. Is the flow of time a feature of the world or of our minds?

cards.title: Possible worlds
cards.text: Philosophers use "possible worlds" to think about what could have been: in some possible world, you became an astronaut.

cards.title: Death and the self
cards.text: Epicurus argued death is nothing to fear: "Where death is, I am not; where I am, death is not." Others find the loss of future goods a real harm.

cards.title: Living in time
cards.text: Seneca wrote that life is long if you know how to use it. Most of us waste time, not lack it.

quiz.q: What gives time its direction in physics?
Who said you can't step in the same river twice?
